title: "Write Taxonomic Descriptions"
format: html

## Overview
  
The `barroso_write_descriptions()` function is a powerful tool in the `barRoso` package for generating automated morphological descriptions from structured Excel data. It transforms taxonomic and morphological character data into standardized, publication-ready species descriptions in Word document format.

## Key Features

- Automatically generates species descriptions from morphological Excel data
- Groups related characters and avoids term repetition
- Combines measurements (length × width) with proper units and symbols
- Formats measurement ranges with en dashes (e.g., "4.3–14.5 cm")
- Writes rare small and large values between parentheses, as usual in taxonomic descriptions (e.g., "(2–)6–40(–55) m")
- Handles complex hierarchical character structures
- Merges duplicate species entries intelligently
- Customizable text formatting (bold, italic) for different description elements
- Exports professionally formatted Word (.docx) documents

## Usage

```r
library(barRoso)

# Generate descriptions for all species
descriptions <- barroso_write_descriptions(
  xlsx_path = "morphological_data.xlsx",
  species_cols = c("Genus", "Species", "Author"),
  character_cols = 4:20
)

# Generate descriptions only for specific species
descriptions <- barroso_write_descriptions(
  xlsx_path = "morphological_data.xlsx",
  species_cols = c("Genus", "Species"),
  character_cols = 3:15,
  species_filter = c("Ouratea concinna", "Ouratea coarctata")
)

# Customize formatting and output
descriptions <- barroso_write_descriptions(
  xlsx_path = "morphological_data.xlsx",
  species_cols = 1:3,
  character_cols = 4:25,
  font_family = "Arial",
  font_size = 11,
  species_bold = TRUE,
  species_italic = TRUE,
  group_bold = FALSE,
  group_italic = TRUE,
  description_bold = FALSE,
  description_italic = FALSE,
  filename = "MySpeciesDescriptions",
  dir = "Output"
)
```

## Output

Returns a data frame with:
  
- species_name: Full species name with authorship
- description_plain: Plain text version of the description

Also creates a Word document (.docx) saved to the specified directory with:
  
Species names formatted following botanical conventions 
Morphological descriptions organized by character groups 
Measurements properly formatted with units
Hierarchical characters grouped logically


## Data Format Requirements

```r
# Excel data should follow these naming conventions:
# Simple characters: "HABIT", "LEAF shape"
# Measurements: "LEAF length (cm)", "LEAF width (mm)"
# Hierarchical: "LEAF MARGINS", "FLOWER SEPALS shape"
# Complex hierarchy: "FLOWER SEPALS BASE shape", "FLOWER SEPALS APEX shape"

# Example data structure:
# | Genus | Species | Author | HABIT | LEAF shape | LEAF length (cm) | LEAF width (cm) |
# |-------|---------|--------|-------|------------|------------------|-----------------|
# | Ouratea | concinna | (Mart.) Engl. | tree | elliptic | 14.5             | 3.8             |
```

## Measurements

Each row of the spreadsheet is one specimen, and each cell of a measurement column has the measurements of that specimen.

### Several measurements of the same specimen

When a specimen was measured more than once for the same character (e.g. several leaves of the same specimen), write the values in the same cell, separated by a vertical bar `|`:

| Genus | Species | Collector | LEAF BLADE length (cm) | LEAF BLADE width (cm) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Ouratea | hostilis | C. Aquino & A.P. Teixeira | 4.3 \| 5 \| 6.5 \| 10.5 | 1 \| 3.5 |
| Ouratea | hostilis | I. Cordeiro | 4.7 \| 6 \| 9.5 | 2.3 \| 3.4 |
| Ouratea | hostilis | C.V. Vidal | 4.8 \| 8 \| 13 | 1 \| 2 |
| Ouratea | hostilis | M.G.Carvalho & S.T.Silva | 9.7 \| 14.5 | 2.6 \| 4.1 |

These are the four specimens of *Ouratea hostilis* in the example dataset `chars_dataset`. The values of all specimens of a species are pooled to build its range. Spaces around the `|` are optional, and a decimal point must be used (`4.5`, not `4,5`).

### Rare values between parentheses

Taxonomic descriptions usually give the common range of a measurement, with rare small and large values between parentheses, e.g. *Tree (2–)6–40 m tall*, *leaflets (7.8–)12–39.5 × (3.7–)5–13(–15.5) cm*. `barroso_write_descriptions()` writes them in two ways:

- **Marked in the spreadsheet**: values written as in a description, e.g. `(5–)7–38(–45)` or `(2–)6 | 9 | 12`, are always written as rare values when they are beyond the range of the other values of the species. Use this when you know a measurement is unusual, even with few specimens.
- **Automatic**: when a species has at least `extremes_min_n` values (default `10`), the range covers the values from the 10th to the 90th percentile (`extremes = c(0.1, 0.9)`), and the smallest and largest values outside it are written between parentheses. The limits of the range are always measured values. For example, the 11 values 2, 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 12, 15, 20, 40 and 55 m become `(2–)6–40(–55) m`. With fewer values, the range goes from the smallest to the largest value (`2–55 m`).

```r
# Percentiles 5 and 95, from 20 values per species
barroso_write_descriptions(xlsx_path = "morphological_data.xlsx",
                           species_cols = c("Genus", "Species", "Author"),
                           character_cols = 4:30,
                           extremes = c(0.05, 0.95),
                           extremes_min_n = 20)

# Just the rare values marked in the spreadsheet
barroso_write_descriptions(xlsx_path = "morphological_data.xlsx",
                           species_cols = c("Genus", "Species", "Author"),
                           character_cols = 4:30,
                           extremes = NULL)
```

### Counts

Counts, like the pairs of secondary veins, the stamens or the flowers of an inflorescence, are also pooled into ranges, with rare values between parentheses, when they are in their own columns with just numbers. Any text goes in another column:

| LEAF SECONDARY-VENATION pairs | LEAF SECONDARY-VENATION | FLOWER STAMEN number | INFLORESCENCE flowers |
|---|---|---|---|
| 6 \| 12 | curved distally towards the marginal vein | 10 | 10 \| 25 |
| 7 \| 9 | curved distally towards the marginal vein | 10 | 15 |

The last word of the column name is written after the range, e.g. *secondary-venation 6–12 pairs, curved distally towards the marginal vein* and *10–25 flowers*, except `number` and `count`, e.g. *stamen 10*. A column of text with numbers, like `6 - 12 pairs, curved distally towards the marginal vein`, is written as it is, and the phrases of the specimens are listed one after the other.

In the *Ouratea* dataset of the dry diagonal of Brazil, most species have 1 to 4 specimens, so automatic rare values appear only where at least 10 measurements were taken, e.g. the leaf blades of *Ouratea hostilis*, with 12 values: `(4.3–)4.7–13(–14.5) × 1–4.1 cm`.

## Examples

# Basic Example

```r
# Using included dataset
data(chars_dataset)
library(openxlsx)
openxlsx::write.xlsx(chars_dataset, "chars_dataset.xlsx")

barroso_write_descriptions(
  xlsx_path = "chars_dataset.xlsx",
  species_cols = c("Genus", "Species", "Author"),
  character_cols = which(names(chars_dataset) == "HABIT"):ncol(chars_dataset)
)
```

# Rare Measurements Between Parentheses

The 12 leaf blade lengths of the four specimens of *Ouratea hostilis* in `chars_dataset` are enough for automatic rare values (`extremes_min_n = 10`), while its leaf blade widths (8 values) and the other measurements keep the full range:

```r
barroso_write_descriptions(
  xlsx_path = "chars_dataset.xlsx",
  species_cols = c("Genus", "Species", "Author"),
  character_cols = which(names(chars_dataset) == "HABIT"):ncol(chars_dataset),
  species_filter = "Ouratea hostilis"
)
```

_**Ouratea hostilis**_ A.Queiroz-Lima & D.B.O.S.Cardoso  
**Shrub or tree** ca. 1.8 m tall; erect; branched; stem striated, scaly, gray, glabrous. **Stipule** 1 pair; lateral to petiole; usually persistent along the branches; 11–16 × 2–3 mm; lanceolate; base truncate; margin entire; apex acute or aristate; glabrous. **Leaf** dispersed; well distributed along the branches; petiole grooved, transverse, glabrous, 0.3–0.5 × 0.1–0.2 cm; blade flat, shiny, membranous, elliptic, lanceolate, **(4.3–)4.7–13(–14.5) × 1–4.1 cm**, apex acute, acuminate, base rounded; …

The leaf blades are 4.7–13 cm long in most measurements, rarely 4.3 or 14.5 cm long.

# Custom Column Selection

```r
# Select specific character groups
selected_cols <- c(
  "HABIT", "HABIT height (m)",
  "LEAF BLADE shape", "LEAF BLADE length (cm)", "LEAF BLADE width (cm)",
  "FLOWER SEPALS shape", "FLOWER SEPALS length (mm)", "FLOWER SEPALS width (mm)"
)

barroso_write_descriptions(
  xlsx_path = "data.xlsx",
  species_cols = c("Genus", "Species"),
  character_cols = selected_cols,
  filename = "Selected_Characters"
)
```

# Using Column Indices

```r
# Use column indices instead of names
barroso_write_descriptions(
  xlsx_path = "data.xlsx",
  species_cols = 1:2,      # First two columns: Genus and Species
  character_cols = 3:18,   # Columns 3-18: morphological characters
  font_family = "Times New Roman",
  font_size = 12
)
```

## Notes

- Uses parsing of column names to group related characters
- Measurements sharing the same base name are automatically combined (e.g., "LEAF length" and "LEAF width" become "X × Y cm")
- ALL CAPS terms in column names are used for hierarchical grouping
- Creates date-stamped folders to organize output by processing date
- Maintains original column order while intelligently grouping related items
